claim: A large-scale screen for aggression-promoting neurons in Drosophila identified several independent hits that enhanced both inter-male aggression and courtship.
source: A large-scale screen for aggression-promoting neurons in Drosophila identified several independent hits that enhanced both inter-male aggression and courtship.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Genetic intersections revealed that 8-10 P1 interneurons, previously thought to exclusively control male courtship, were sufficient to promote fighting.
source: Genetic intersections revealed that 8-10 P1 interneurons, previously thought to exclusively control male courtship, were sufficient to promote fighting.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by split-GAL4 intersection experiments shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: P1 activation could promote aggression at a threshold below that required for wing extension.
source: Optogenetic experiments indicated that P1 activation could promote aggression at a threshold below that required for wing extension.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by optogenetic experiments in Figure 3.

claim: P1 activation in the absence of wing extension triggered persistent aggression via an internal state that could endure for minutes.
source: P1 activation in the absence of wing extension triggered persistent aggression via an internal state that could endure for minutes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by barrier experiments in Figure 5.

claim: High-frequency P1 activation promoted wing extension and suppressed aggression during photostimulation.
source: High-frequency P1 activation promoted wing extension and suppressed aggression during photostimulation, whereas aggression resumed and wing extension was inhibited following photostimulation offset.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in optogenetic experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Aggression resumed and wing extension was inhibited following photostimulation offset.
source: High-frequency P1 activation promoted wing extension and suppressed aggression during photostimulation, whereas aggression resumed and wing extension was inhibited following photostimulation offset.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: P1 neuron activation promotes a latent, internal state that facilitates aggression and courtship.
source: Thus, P1 neuron activation promotes a latent, internal state that facilitates aggression and courtship, and controls the overt expression of these social behaviors in a threshold-dependent, inverse manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments throughout the paper.

claim: P1 neurons control the overt expression of aggression and courtship in a threshold-dependent, inverse manner.
source: Thus, P1 neuron activation promotes a latent, internal state that facilitates aggression and courtship, and controls the overt expression of these social behaviors in a threshold-dependent, inverse manner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by optogenetic experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Aggression is an innate social behavior that is critical for survival and reproduction in most sexually propagating metazoan species.
source: Aggression is an innate social behavior that is critical for survival and reproduction in most sexually propagating metazoan species (Lorenz, 1966).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Lorenz, 1966.

claim: Aggression serves to establish dominance, or to defend or obtain resources, territory or mating partners.
source: It serves to establish dominance, or to defend or obtain resources, territory or mating partners.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about aggression.

claim: Maladaptive aggression in humans takes an enormous toll on society.
source: While it is part of most animals' normal behavioral repertoire, maladaptive aggression in humans takes an enormous toll on society (Filley et al., 2001; Miczek et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Classical experiments in cats and rodents revealed the existence of localized 'centers' in the medial hypothalamus, whose artificial electrical stimulation was sufficient to trigger attack behavior.
source: Classical experiments in cats and rodents revealed the existence of localized 'centers' in the medial hypothalamus, whose artificial electrical stimulation was sufficient to trigger attack behavior (Hess, 1928; Hess and Brügger, 1943; reviewed in Siegel et al., 1999; Kruk, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations to classical studies.

claim: Neurons responsible for hypothalamic aggression centers were identified in the murine ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), using steroid hormone receptors as molecular markers, and optogenetics.
source: Recently, the neurons responsible for this activity were identified in the murine ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), using steroid hormone receptors as molecular markers, and optogenetics (Lin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2014) or genetically targeted cell ablation (Yang et al., 2013; reviewed in Falkner and Lin, 2014; Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to recent studies.

claim: VMH neurons number approximately 2,000 per hemisphere.
source: Interestingly, although these cells number ~2,000 per hemisphere, they play a role in male-female mating behavior as well as in fighting (Lin et al., 2011; Sano et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: VMH neurons play a role in male-female mating behavior as well as in fighting.
source: Interestingly, although these cells number ~2,000 per hemisphere, they play a role in male-female mating behavior as well as in fighting (Lin et al., 2011; Sano et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster presents an attractive alternative model for dissecting the neural circuitry of aggression because of the reduced complexity of its nervous system and the availability of genetic tools.
source: Drosophila melanogaster presents an attractive alternative model for dissecting the neural circuitry of aggression, because of the reduced complexity of its nervous system and the availability of genetic tools for marking and manipulating specific neuronal cell types (Baier et al., 2002; Kravitz and Huber, 2003; Zwarts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Drosophila males exhibit robust aggressive behavior, which consists of different agonistic actions such as wing threat, lunging, tussling and boxing.
source: Drosophila males exhibit robust aggressive behavior, which consists of different agonistic actions such as wing threat, lunging, tussling and boxing (Dow and von Schilcher, 1975; Skrzipek et al., 1979; Hoffmann, 1987; Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Aggression in flies reflects competition over resources such as food, territory or females.
source: Aggression in flies, as in other species, reflects competition over resources such as food, territory or females (Hoffmann and Cacoyianni, 1990; Chen et al., 2002; Hoyer et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014), and is under genetic control (Dierick and Greenspan, 2006; Zwarts et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Aggression in flies is under genetic control.
source: Aggression in flies, as in other species, reflects competition over resources such as food, territory or females (Hoffmann and Cacoyianni, 1990; Chen et al., 2002; Hoyer et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014), and is under genetic control (Dierick and Greenspan, 2006; Zwarts et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The male-specific form of the sex-determination gene fruitless (fruM) is required for normal intermale aggression in Drosophila.
source: The male-specific form of the sex-determination gene fruitless (fruM) is required for normal intermale aggression in Drosophila (Vrontou et al., 2006) and genetic feminization of relatively broad neuronal populations can feminize (Nilsen et al., 2004) aggressive behavior (Certel et al., 2007; Chan and Kravitz, 2007; Mundiyanapurath et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: DTKFruM neurons represent the first subclass of FruM-expressing neurons that appears specific to the control of aggression.
source: Thus, DTKFruM neurons represent the first subclass of FruM-expressing neurons that appears specific to the control of aggression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Of the 3038 lines screened, 815 lines had phenotypes that interfered with the ability to engage in social behaviors.
source: Of the 3038 lines screened (Figure 1A), 815 lines had phenotypes that interfered with the ability to engage in social behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the screen.

claim: 19 GAL4 lines showed a significant increase in one or more aggressive behaviors compared to the control line.
source: Of the remaining lines, 19 showed a significant increase in one or more aggressive behaviors, compared to an enhancer-less GAL4 control line BDPG4U (pBDPGAL4u; Pfeiffer et al., 2010) (Figure 1A and B), which does not drive expression in the central nervous system (CNS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Three GAL4 lines exhibited both increased aggression and increased inter-male courtship measured as unilateral wing extension.
source: Interestingly, three of these aggression-promoting lines, including R15A01-GAL4, R71G01-GAL4 and R22G11-GAL4, also displayed a robust increase in courtship behavior as measured by wing extension (Figure 1B, inset; Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The P1a spGAL4 driver labeled approximately 8–10 FruM-expressing P1 neurons per hemibrain.
source: Indeed, the spGAL4 intersection of R15A01-AD and R71G01-DBD (henceforth referred to as P1a spGAL4) labeled approximately 8–10 FruM-expressing P1 neurons per hemibrain (see also Inagaki et al., 2013); no labeling was observed in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The P1a spGAL4 driver labeled a minor and variable population of neurons (<4 per hemibrain) with cell bodies in the lateral horn (LH) that were neither FruM-positive nor male-specific.
source: In addition to P1 neurons, the P1a spGAL4 driver labeled a minor and variable population of neurons (<4 per hemibrain) with cell bodies in the lateral horn (LH) that were neither FruM-positive nor male-specific (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: dTrpA1 activation of P1a spGAL4 males resulted in a robust, temperature-dependent increase in both aggression and wing extension.
source: Strikingly, dTrpA1 activation of P1a spGAL4 males resulted in a robust, temperature-dependent increase in both aggression and wing extension (Figure 1F), compared to a control intersection of R15A01-AD and a driverless-DBD line (BDP-DBD).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: P1a>dTrpA1 males showed a significant increase in lunging towards wild-type target males throughout the observation period.
source: In such mixed-genotype pairs, P1a>dTrpA1 males still showed a significant increase in lunging towards the WT target male throughout the observation period, in comparison to BDPG4U>dTrpA1 controls (Figures 1G, lower and 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: The lunging frequency per P1a>dTrpA1 male was not significantly different between same genotype and mixed-genotype pairs.
source: The lunging frequency per P1a>dTrpA1 male was not significantly different between same genotype (P1a vs P1a) and mixed-genotype pairs (P1a vs WT) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1H.

claim: Wild-type target males showed no significant lunging behavior towards the P1a>dTrpA1 aggressor.
source: In contrast, the WT target males (identified by clipping the tip of one wing) showed no significant lunging behavior towards the P1a>dTrpA1 aggressor (Figure 1H, left panel, Tester: WT).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1H.

claim: The sustained increase in aggression caused by activating P1a neurons in a mixed pair does not depend on counter-attack by the target fly.
source: These data indicate that the sustained increase in aggression caused by activating P1a neurons in a mixed pair does not depend on counter-attack by the target fly.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the mixed-genotype pair experiments.

claim: Increased male wing extension behavior is neither necessary nor sufficient to explain the increased aggression phenotype.
source: These data indicate that increased male wing extension behavior is neither necessary nor sufficient to explain the increased aggression phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on multiple experiments.

claim: The aggression phenotype reflects a fly-intrinsic influence of P1a neuron activation.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the aggression phenotype reflects a fly-intrinsic influence of P1a neuron activation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on multiple experiments.

claim: All intersectional flies with FruM+ P1 neurons exhibited a significant increase in lunging upon dTrpA1 activation.
source: Despite the small number of P1 neurons labeled, all of these intersectional flies exhibited a significant increase in lunging upon dTrpA1 activation (Figures 2E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 2E and F.

claim: There was little to no enhancement of wing extension in FruM+ P1 neuron intersectional flies.
source: In contrast to the enhanced aggression, however, there was little to no enhancement of wing extension (Figures 2E and G), consistent with earlier reports that at least 10 P1 neurons must express dTrpA1myc to significantly increase singing relative to controls (von Philipsborn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 2E and G and citation to von Philipsborn et al., 2011.

claim: Activation of just a few FruM P1 neurons is sufficient to increase aggression.
source: These observations indicate that activation of just a few FruM P1 neurons is sufficient to increase aggression.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the FruM+ P1 neuron experiments.

claim: Increased aggression can be observed in the absence of elevated wing extension.
source: They also demonstrate that the increased aggression phenotype can be observed in the absence of elevated wing extension, further dissociating these two behavioral phenotypes of P1 neuron activation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the FruM+ P1 neuron experiments.

claim: A linear increase in the magnitude of GCaMP6s responses from each P1 neuron was observed as the photostimulation frequency was increased from 10 to 50 Hz.
source: We observed a linear increase in the magnitude of GCaMP6s responses from each P1 neuron as the PS frequency was increased from 10 to 50 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: As the photostimulation frequency was increased from 1 to 20 Hz, there was a progressive increase in lunging rate by P1a>CsChrimson vs. BDPG4U>CsChrimson control flies.
source: In freely behaving male fly pairs, as the PS frequency was increased from 1 to 20 Hz, there was a progressive increase in lunging rate by P1a>CsChrimson vs. BDPG4U>CsChrimson control flies (Figures 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 3A and B.

claim: At 10 Hz and above, the lunging rate was significantly higher than that of genetic controls stimulated at the same frequency.
source: At 10 Hz and above (the threshold frequency that yielded a significant increase in GCaMP6 responses; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) the lunging rate was significantly higher than that of genetic controls stimulated at the same frequency (Figure 3C, blue vs. white bars), and of pre-stimulation baseline lunging levels in the experimental genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The enhancement of aggression in P1a>CsChrimson flies was not time-locked to the onset of photostimulation, but rather tended to increase following photostimulation offset.
source: However, the enhancement of aggression in P1a>CsChrimson flies was not time-locked to the onset of PS, but rather tended to increase following PS offset (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Across the photostimulation frequency range of 1–20 Hz, there was little promotion of wing extension.
source: Importantly, across this same frequency range (1–20 Hz) there was little promotion of wing extension (Figures 3A and D, red lines/bars; Figure 3F, red lines).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 3A, D, and F.

claim: The threshold for optogenetic enhancement of aggression by P1a neurons is lower than that required for wing extension.
source: These data indicate that the threshold for optogenetic enhancement of aggression by P1a neurons is lower than that required for wing extension, under these conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Aggression was increasingly suppressed during the light ON phase as the photostimulation frequency was raised above the threshold for evoking wing extension.
source: As the PS frequency was raised above the threshold for evoking wing extension, we observed that aggression was increasingly suppressed during the light ON phase (Figure 3C, 30–50 Hz, shaded regions; Figure 3G, 'ON'; Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C and 3G.

claim: Following photostimulation offset, aggression rapidly resumed and wing extension was concomitantly suppressed.
source: Following PS offset, however, aggression rapidly resumed and wing extension was concomitantly suppressed (Figures 3A and C, 30–50 Hz, blue bars; Figure 3G; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2E for 50 Hz PS; Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 3A, C, and G.

claim: High-frequency P1 activation promoted extended periods of locomotor arrest, which was relieved following photostimulation offset.
source: We also observed that high-frequency P1 activation promoted extended periods of locomotor arrest, which was relieved following PS offset (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: A relatively rapid decline of wing extension was observed following the offset of high-frequency photostimulation.
source: Conversely, we observed a relatively rapid decline of wing extension following the offset of high-frequency PS (Figures 3A and D, red; 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E; t1/2 = 9 ± 3 s), concomitant with the re-initiation of aggression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 3A, D, and G.

claim: Silencing of TKFruM neurons strongly suppressed the enhancement of lunging that occurred following termination of P1 photoactivation.
source: Indeed, silencing of TKFruM neurons using Kir2.1 (Baines et al., 2001) strongly suppressed the enhancement of lunging that occurred following termination of P1 photoactivation (Figure 3H, lunging, blue box and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, bottom raster).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: TKFruM neurons are either functionally downstream of P1 neurons, or act in a parallel pathway required for aggression.
source: This result indicates that TKFruM neurons are either functionally downstream of P1 neurons, or act in a parallel pathway required for aggression.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the epistasis experiment.

claim: Silencing TKFruM neurons caused a strong and statistically significant increase in wing extension during the light OFF period.
source: Strikingly, although silencing TKFruM neurons had no effect to diminish or enhance wing extension during PS (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B), it caused a strong and statistically significant increase in wing extension during the light OFF period (Figure 3H, right, red box; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, bottom raster).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Silencing of TKFruM neurons in male pairs allowed P1a activation-induced wing extension to persist into the post-stimulation period, similar to the response of solitary flies.
source: In other words, silencing of TKFruM neurons in male pairs allowed P1a activation-induced wing extension to persist into the post-stimulation period, similar to the response of solitary flies (Inagaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Inagaki et al., 2013.

claim: The rapid decrease in wing extension observed following the offset of photostimulation is caused by the resumption of aggression.
source: These data indicate that the rapid decrease in wing extension observed following the offset of photostimulation (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) is indeed caused by the resumption of aggression.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the epistasis experiment.

claim: A significant reduction in the frequency of lunging following transient P1a photoactivation was observed when P1a>ReaChR males were paired with target males lacking oenocytes.
source: Under these conditions, a significant reduction in the frequency of lunging following transient P1a photoactivation was observed, in comparison to P1a>ReaChR males paired with control male targets bearing intact oenocytes (oe+) (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3I.

claim: The abrupt switch from enhanced wing extension to enhanced fighting following the offset of P1a activation requires appropriate chemosensory cues on the conspecific target.
source: Thus, the abrupt switch from enhanced wing extension to enhanced fighting following the offset of P1a activation requires appropriate chemosensory cues on the conspecific target.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the oenocyte ablation experiment.

claim: Ongoing aggression was observed in the 1 min intervals between successive episodes of high-frequency P1a neuron activation.
source: The fact that ongoing aggression was observed in the 1 min intervals between successive episodes of high-frequency P1a neuron activation (Figure 3A) indicated that this behavior, once triggered, could be sustained at least briefly without continued PS.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Wing extension was robustly induced during photostimulation but switched to aggression following photostimulation offset in P1a>ReaChR male pairs exposed to one 1-min episode of photoactivation.
source: Under these conditions, wing extension was robustly induced during PS, but switched to aggression following PS offset; this lunging persisted for at least 10 min (Figures 4A−C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 4A-C.

claim: Robust, persistent aggression could be triggered by weaker photostimulation conditions that promoted only occasional wing extension bouts in a subset of flies.
source: Such robust, persistent aggression could also be triggered by weaker photosimulation conditions that promoted only occasional wing extension bouts in a subset of flies (Figures 4D−F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 4D-F.

claim: Persistent post-photostimulation aggression was triggered even in the cohort of fly pairs that showed no wing extension at all during the photostimulation period.
source: Under these latter conditions, persistent post-PS aggression was triggered even in the cohort of fly pairs (8/22) that showed no wing extension at all during the PS period (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Persistent aggression could be promoted by a single episode of P1a neuronal activation, and did not depend on male-male wing extension behavior during photostimulation.
source: Thus, persistent aggression could be promoted by a single episode of P1a neuronal activation, and did not depend on male-male wing extension behavior during PS.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Persistent attack towards a wild-type target lasting at least 10 min was triggered by a single episode of photostimulation when P1a>ReaChR flies were paired with a group-housed, non-aggressive wild-type target fly.
source: Under these conditions, persistent attack towards the WT target lasting at least 10 min was triggered by a single episode of photostimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Persistent aggression was not simply perpetuated by self-sustaining cycles of attack and counter-attack, but likely reflected a long-lived internal state in the tester fly.
source: These results suggested that persistent aggression was not simply perpetuated by self-sustaining cycles of attack and counter-attack, but likely reflected a long-lived internal state in the tester fly.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the mixed-genotype pair experiments.

claim: Separated P1a>ReaChR males showed a robust increase in wing extension during photostimulation, which persisted after light offset.
source: As expected, separated P1a>ReaChR males (Figure 5B), but not BDPG4U>ReaChR males (Figure 5C), showed a robust increase in wing extension during PS, which persisted after light offset (Inagaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 5B and C and citation to Inagaki et al., 2013.

claim: Upon removal of the barrier 1 min after photostimulation offset, P1a>ReaChR males switched to aggression.
source: Upon removal of the barrier 1 min after PS offset (a time when the flies were still performing wing extensions), these P1a >ReaChR males switched to aggression (Figures 5B, blue rasters).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Enhanced aggression was observed even when removal of the barrier was delayed for 10 min after the offset of photostimulation.
source: Strikingly, enhanced aggression was observed even when removal of the barrier was delayed for 10 min after the offset of PS (Figures 5D and E) (Video 5), by which time persistent wing extension behavior (Figure 5F), as well as locomotor activity (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), had decayed to baseline levels for at least 5 min.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 5D, E, and F.

claim: The level of lunging after barrier removal for both the 1 min and 10 min conditions was significantly elevated compared to BDPG4U>ReaChR controls.
source: The level of lunging after barrier removal for both the 1 min and 10 min conditions was significantly elevated compared to BDPG4U>ReaChR controls (Figure 5G), as well as control P1a>ReaChR males that received no PS (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 5G and H.

claim: The latency to lunging was not significantly different between barrier removal at 1 min vs. 10 min.
source: Although the latency to lunging was not significantly different between barrier removal at 1 min vs. 10 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), the flies took longer to achieve maximal levels of aggression in the latter case, suggestive of a decay in the internal state promoted by P1a activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: P1 neuron activation triggers a persistent internal state facilitating future social behaviors, which can endure for minutes in behaviorally quiescent solitary flies.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that P1 neuron activation triggers a persistent internal state facilitating future social behaviors, which can endure for minutes in behaviorally quiescent solitary flies.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the barrier experiments.

claim: The identification of P1 neurons in a screen for aggression-promoting neurons was surprising, as the prevailing view is that these cells specifically promote male courtship behavior.
source: The identification of P1 neurons in a screen for aggression-promoting neurons was surprising, as the prevailing view is that these cells specifically promote male courtship behavior, in response to female-specific pheromones (Kohatsu et al., 2011; von Philipsborn et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2012; Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: Activation of P1 neurons promotes aggression in a fly-intrinsic manner, and is not an indirect social response provoked by elevated wing extension behavior.
source: These data suggest that activation of P1 neurons promotes aggression in a fly-intrinsic manner, and is not an indirect social response provoked by elevated wing extension behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion based on the experimental results.

claim: Attempts to demonstrate a requirement for P1 neurons during spontaneous aggression using various methods of cell inactivation or ablation have been unsuccessful.
source: Unfortunately, attempts to demonstrate a requirement for P1 neurons during spontaneous aggression using various methods of cell inactivation or ablation have so far been unsuccessful.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: While artificial activation of P1 neurons can promote aggression, it remains unclear whether they are normally required for this behavior.
source: Thus, while artificial activation of P1 neurons can promote aggression, it remains unclear whether they are normally required for this behavior, and if so under what circumstances.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat in the discussion.

claim: The effect of P1 neurons to promote aggression vs. wing extension could be uncoupled by systematically manipulating the level of activation using red-shifted optogenetic effectors.
source: We found that the effect of P1 neurons to promote aggression vs. wing extension could be uncoupled, by systematically manipulating the level of activation using red-shifted optogenetic effectors.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claim: At low frequencies of photostimulation (≤20 Hz), a modest but significant increase in aggression was evoked, without any accompanying increase in unilateral wing extension behavior.
source: At low frequencies of photostimulation (≤20 Hz), a modest but significant increase in aggression was evoked, without any accompanying increase in unilateral wing extension behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Wing extension was evoked at photostimulation frequencies above 30 Hz.
source: Wing extension was evoked at photostimulation frequencies above 30 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Output from the P1 population can control different behaviors at different thresholds.
source: These data suggest that output from the P1 population can control different behaviors at different thresholds.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion based on the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Studies of hypothalamic circuits in mice have revealed a threshold-dependent influence of optogenetic activation on mating and aggression.
source: Nevertheless, it is of interest that studies of hypothalamic circuits in mice have also revealed a threshold-dependent influence of optogenetic activation on mating and aggression (although opposite to the direction observed here) (Hong et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: At high stimulation frequencies (≥30 Hz), wing extension was promoted during the light ON phase, while aggression was suppressed.
source: The temporal resolution afforded by optogenetic activation of P1 neurons also revealed an inverse relationship between the promotion of these two behaviors: at high stimulation frequencies (≥30 Hz), wing extension was promoted during the light ON phase, while aggression was suppressed; conversely, during the light OFF phase, aggression resumed and wing extension was suppressed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claim: During the light OFF phase, aggression resumed and wing extension was suppressed.
source: The temporal resolution afforded by optogenetic activation of P1 neurons also revealed an inverse relationship between the promotion of these two behaviors: at high stimulation frequencies (≥30 Hz), wing extension was promoted during the light ON phase, while aggression was suppressed; conversely, during the light OFF phase, aggression resumed and wing extension was suppressed.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claim: When aggression is inhibited by silencing TK-GAL41 neurons, wing extension triggered by optogenetic activation of P1a neurons persists into the light OFF phase.
source: Our cellular epistasis experiment revealed that when aggression is inhibited, by silencing TK-GAL41 neurons (Asahina et al., 2014), wing extension triggered by optogenetic activation of P1a neurons persists into the light OFF phase, as described previously for single male flies (Inagaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to Asahina et al., 2014 and Inagaki et al., 2013.

claim: Aggressive behavior causally suppresses wing extension following the offset of photostimulation.
source: This result indicates that aggressive behavior causally suppresses wing extension following the offset of photostimulation, suggestive of an inhibitory influence at the neural circuit or behavioral level.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion based on the epistasis experiment.

claim: The suppression of lunging during the light ON phase may reflect a reciprocal inhibitory influence of courtship circuitry on aggression.
source: By extension, the suppression of lunging during the light ON phase may reflect a reciprocal inhibitory influence of courtship circuitry on aggression (however, the acute suppression of locomotor activity produced by strong optogenetic activation of P1 neurons may contribute to the inhibition of aggression as well).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: Reciprocal inhibitory influences between circuits controlling 'opponent' behaviors is well established.
source: The existence of reciprocal inhibitory influences between circuits controlling 'opponent' behaviors is well established (reviewed in Kristan, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Kristan, 2008.

claim: Transient activation of P1 neurons triggers persistent wing extension in solitary males.
source: Previously, it was shown that transient activation of P1 neurons triggers persistent wing extension in solitary males (Inagaki et al., 2013; Bath et al., 2014; Clowney et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: Transient activation of P1 neurons can result in enhanced aggression, even when physical contact between the flies was delayed for 10 min.
source: This experiment revealed that transient activation of P1 neurons could result in enhanced aggression, even when physical contact between the flies was delayed for 10 min, long after persistent singing had decayed to baseline.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the barrier experiments.

claim: Activation of P1 neurons can induce a persistent, fly-intrinsic internal state that facilitates future social behavior.
source: Thus, activation of P1 neurons can induce a persistent, fly-intrinsic internal state (e.g., of arousal or motivation) that facilitates future social behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion based on the barrier experiments.

claim: The P1-induced persistent internal state does not simply reflect a state of generalized arousal.
source: This state can endure without any increase in locomotor activity, suggesting that it does not simply reflect a state of generalized arousal (van Swinderen and Andretic, 2003); however, it is difficult to prove that it exclusively influences social behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to van Swinderen and Andretic, 2003.

claim: Activation of P1 neurons themselves did not appear to trigger long-lasting persistent activity within this population, as measured by calcium imaging.
source: Activation of P1 neurons themselves did not appear to trigger long-lasting persistent activity within this population, as measured by calcium imaging (Inagaki et al., 2013 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to Inagaki et al., 2013 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of P1 neurons never triggered aggression in a stimulus-locked manner during the light ON phase.
source: We observed that optogenetic activation of P1 neurons never triggered aggression in a stimulus-locked manner during the light ON phase, even during low frequency stimulation where no wing extension behavior was evoked; rather an increase in aggression was typically observed following PS offset (Figure 3, 10 Hz and 20 Hz).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Male flies fight only in the presence of an appetitive resource, such as food and/or mating partners.
source: Male flies fight only in the presence of an appetitive resource, such as food and/or mating partners (Jacobs, 1978; Hoffmann, 1987; Chen et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: P1 neurons are activated by even brief contact with a female.
source: Since P1 neurons are activated by even brief contact with a female (Kohatsu et al., 2011; Clowney et al., 2015; Kohatsu and Yamamoto, 2015), the persistent internal state they engender by this low-level activation could provide an enduring representation of this resource—i.e., a memory of a mating partner.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to Kohatsu et al., 2011; Clowney et al., 2015; Kohatsu and Yamamoto, 2015.

claim: The persistent internal state engendered by P1 activation could provide an enduring representation of a mating partner.
source: Since P1 neurons are activated by even brief contact with a female (Kohatsu et al., 2011; Clowney et al., 2015; Kohatsu and Yamamoto, 2015), the persistent internal state they engender by this low-level activation could provide an enduring representation of this resource—i.e., a memory of a mating partner.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: The inhibitory influence of acute P1 activation on fighting may serve to suppress aggression towards a female when a male fly is directly engaged in courtship or mating behavior.
source: At the same time, the inhibitory influence of acute P1 activation on fighting may serve to suppress aggression towards a female when a male fly is directly engaged in courtship or mating behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: P1 neurons could exert both inhibitory and facilitatory influences on aggression, albeit on different time scales.
source: In this way, P1 neurons could exert both inhibitory and facilitatory influences on aggression, albeit on different time scales.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: Tinbergen proposed that behavioral decisions are made in a hierarchical manner.
source: Tinbergen (Tinbergen, 1951) proposed that such decisions are made in a hierarchical manner.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Tinbergen, 1951.

claim: A clear prediction of Tinbergen's model is the existence of a 'higher-level' circuit node that controls multiple reproductive behaviors, including aggression and courtship.
source: Although this model has relatively limited experimental support (Pirger et al., 2014), a clear prediction is the existence of a 'higher-level' circuit node (or module) that controls multiple reproductive behaviors, including aggression and courtship.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Pirger et al., 2014.

claim: The discovery of a small cluster of neurons in Drosophila that collectively can control both fighting and mating behavior appears consistent with Tinbergen's prediction.
source: Our discovery of a small cluster of neurons in Drosophila that collectively can control both fighting and mating behavior appears consistent with this prediction.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: Tinbergen proposed that common modules would be the site at which internal state influences exerted their effects to promote behavioral arousal or motivation.
source: Tinbergen also proposed that such common modules would be the site at which internal state influences exerted their effects to promote behavioral arousal or motivation (Tinbergen, 1951).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Tinbergen, 1951.

claim: The finding that P1 neurons promote a persistent internal state that facilitates both courtship and aggression is consistent with Tinbergen's proposal.
source: Our finding that P1 neurons promote a persistent internal state that facilitates both courtship and aggression would seem consistent with this proposal as well.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: A relatively small population of neurons in the mouse hypothalamus controls mating and fighting.
source: The independent discovery of a relatively small population of neurons that controls mating and fighting in the mouse hypothalamus (Lin et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014), moreover, suggests that such common nodes may represent an evolutionarily conserved circuit 'motif' for the organization and control of innate social behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to Lin et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014.

claim: Common nodes controlling mating and fighting may represent an evolutionarily conserved circuit 'motif' for the organization and control of innate social behaviors.
source: The independent discovery of a relatively small population of neurons that controls mating and fighting in the mouse hypothalamus (Lin et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014), moreover, suggests that such common nodes may represent an evolutionarily conserved circuit 'motif' for the organization and control of innate social behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion with citations.

claim: 3038 GAL4 lines were screened in the thermogenetic activation screen.
source: Of the 3038 lines screened (Figure 1A), 815 lines had phenotypes that interfered with the ability to engage in social behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The screen yielded approximately 20 hits exhibiting elevated aggression, indicating a high level of specificity.
source: Thermogenetic activation of ~3,000 Drosophila GAL4 lines (Jenett et al., 2012) using the temperature-sensitive cation channel dTrpA1 (Hamada et al., 2008) yielded ~20 hits exhibiting elevated aggression, indicating a high level of specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: Three hits from the screen labeled a common subset of P1 neurons.
source: Remarkably, intersectional experiments using the split-GAL4 technique revealed that the P1 neurons were virtually the only cells in common between these three hits, and, moreover, that these neurons were responsible for both the aggression and wing extension phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: P1 neurons were independently recovered in three independent hits, constituting only 0.1% of the lines initially screened.
source: The fact that P1 neurons were independently recovered in three independent hits, constituting only 0.1% of the lines initially screened, and could be isolated from 'contaminating' cell types by carrying out pair-wise intersectional combinations of these hits (Luan et al., 2006; Pfeiffer et al., 2010), testifies to the reproducibility of the phenotype and the power of the screen to reveal rare populations of neurons that control social behavior in Drosophila.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.
